[Athens](/wiki/Athens "Athens") was chosen as the host city during the 106th IOC Session held in [Lausanne](/wiki/Lausanne "Lausanne"), Switzerland, on 5 September 1997. The Greek capital had lost its bid to organize the [1996 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") to the American city of [Atlanta](/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") nearly seven years before, during the 96th IOC Session in Tokyo, Japan on 18 September 1990. Under the direction of [Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki](/wiki/Gianna_Angelopoulos-Daskalaki "Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki"), Athens pursued another bid, this time for the right to host the Summer Olympics in 2004. The success of Athens in securing the 2004 Games was based largely on the bid's appeal to human values, the history of the Games from ancient age and modern age and the emphasis that Athens is placed at the pivotal role that Greece and Athens could play in promoting the Modern Olympism and the Olympic Movement.[[7]](#cite_note-9) Unlike the 1996 bid that was seen arrogant when the city was bidding, the 2004 bid was lauded for its low scale, humility, honest and earnestness, its focused message, and a more real and detailed bid concept.[[8]](#cite_note-10)

The [University of Indonesia](/wiki/University_of_Indonesia "University of Indonesia") (UI), one of the country's oldest and largest public universities, operates campuses in Salemba, Central Jakarta, and nearby Depok.[[157]](#cite_note-160) Other public universities in the capital region include [Syarif Hidayatullah State Islamic University Jakarta](/wiki/Syarif_Hidayatullah_State_Islamic_University_Jakarta "Syarif Hidayatullah State Islamic University Jakarta") and the [State University of Jakarta](/wiki/State_University_of_Jakarta "State University of Jakarta") (UNJ).[[158]](#cite_note-161)

The city also hosts numerous private universities and colleges. Major institutions include [Trisakti University](/wiki/Trisakti_University "Trisakti University"), [Atma Jaya University](/wiki/Atma_Jaya_Catholic_University_of_Indonesia "Atma Jaya Catholic University of Indonesia"), among others. Modern higher education in the city can be traced in part to colonial-era medical training in Batavia beginning in 1851, which later developed into [STOVIA](/wiki/STOVIA "STOVIA") (*School tot Opleiding van Indische Artsen*).[[156]](#cite_note-Pols-159) Students in Jakarta commonly live in dormitories, boarding houses (*kost*), or other rented accommodation while studying.[[159]](#cite_note-162)

This is thought to be the first telescopic observation of moons other than Earth's. Just one day after Galileo, [Simon Marius](/wiki/Simon_Marius "Simon Marius") independently discovered moons around Jupiter, though he did not publish his discovery in a book until 1614.[[183]](#cite_note-189) It was Marius's names for the major moons, however, that stuck: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. The discovery was a major point in favour of the [heliocentric](/wiki/Heliocentrism "Heliocentrism") theory of the motions of the planets by [Nicolaus Copernicus](/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus "Nicolaus Copernicus"); Galileo's outspoken support of the Copernican theory led to him being tried and condemned by the [Inquisition](/wiki/Inquisition "Inquisition").[[184]](#cite_note-190)

In the autumn of 1639, the Neapolitan optician Francesco Fontana tested a 22-palm telescope of his own making and discovered the characteristic bands of the planet's atmosphere.[[185]](#cite_note-191)

**Bordeaux wine** ([Occitan](/wiki/Occitan_language "Occitan language"): *vin de Bordèu*; [French](/wiki/French_language "French language"): *vin de Bordeaux*) is produced in the [Bordeaux region](/wiki/Bordeaux_wine_regions "Bordeaux wine regions") of southwest [France](/wiki/France "France"), around the city of [Bordeaux](/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), on the [Garonne River](/wiki/Garonne "Garonne"). To the north of the city, the [Dordogne River](/wiki/Dordogne_(river) "Dordogne (river)") joins the [Garonne](/wiki/Garonne "Garonne") forming the broad estuary called the [Gironde](/wiki/Gironde_estuary "Gironde estuary"); the [Gironde](/wiki/Gironde "Gironde") department, with a total vineyard area of 110,800 hectares,[[1]](#cite_note-1) is the second largest wine-growing area in France behind the Languedoc-Rousillon.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Average vintages produce over 700 million bottles of wine, ranging from large quantities of daily [table wine](/wiki/Table_wine "Table wine") to some of the world's most expensive and prestigious wines. The vast majority of wine produced in Bordeaux is red (sometimes called "claret" in Britain), with sweet white wines (most notably [Sauternes](/wiki/Sauternes_(wine) "Sauternes (wine)")), dry whites, and (in much smaller quantities) rosé and sparkling wines ([Crémant de Bordeaux](/wiki/Cr%C3%A9mant_de_Bordeaux "Crémant de Bordeaux")) collectively making up the remainder. Bordeaux wine is made by more than 5,660 producers or *[châteaux](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau "Château")*. There are 65 [appellations](/wiki/Appellation_d%27origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e "Appellation d'origine contrôlée") of Bordeaux wine.[[3]](#cite_note-Bordeaux_Figures-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Judge Jackson at the James B. Parsons Legacy Dinner on February 24, 2020

Jackson has said she does not have a particular judicial philosophy,[[144]](#cite_note-brookings-144) but rather has a perspective on legal analysis or a "judicial methodology".[[145]](#cite_note-145)[[146]](#cite_note-Harvard-146) Though she has not embraced the label, Jackson has expressed that she sees value in [originalism](/wiki/Originalism "Originalism"), saying the "Constitution is fixed in its meaning", and has explicitly criticized [living constitutionalism](/wiki/Living_constitutionalism "Living constitutionalism").[[146]](#cite_note-Harvard-146)

In January 2022, *The New York Times* reported that Jackson had "not yet written a body of appeals court opinions expressing a legal philosophy" because she had joined the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in the summer of 2021. However, *The Times* said, Jackson's earlier rulings "comported with those of a liberal-leaning judge", including her opinions blocking various Trump administration actions.[[8]](#cite_note-nyt-8) Additionally, a review of over 500 of her judicial opinions indicated that she would likely be as liberal as Breyer, the justice she replaced.[[147]](#cite_note-147)

According to Sahil Kapur, writing for [NBC News](/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News"), "Jackson fits well with the Democratic Party and the progressive movement's agenda" due to her relative youth, background as a public defender, and history of labor-friendly rulings.[[148]](#cite_note-148)

*[Politico](/wiki/Politico "Politico")* reported that "Jackson is popular with liberal legal activists looking to replace Breyer with a justice willing to engage in ideological combat with the court's conservatives."[[149]](#cite_note-149)
